news.title: Butane’s Perfect Storm Sends Prices to Decade Highs
news.summary: Butane prices are surging across the world. Northwest European November butane prices have reached $1,125/t by early November, their highest level in 30 years, having exceeded even the peaks following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. In Asia, the AFEI butane index stood at $1,180/t on November 3. US butane Belvieu prices have climbed to a 14-year high $920/t. This surge in prices reflects several overlapping trends, with the most significant being a reorientation of global propane/butane trade flows since the US-Iran war kicked off in March.…

analysis.summary: Global butane prices hit multi-year and multi-decade highs due to wartime trade flow disruptions and tightening energy supplies.
analysis.rationale: Surging NGL prices reflect tightening hydrocarbon and refined product supply chains, exerting upward price pressure across the broader petroleum complex, though butane-specific evidence provides only limited direct confirmation for crude.

news.title: Oil Crashes 9% as Trump and Vance Blame Iran War for Midterm Rout
news.summary: Brent fell $8.94, or 8.6%, to $94.66 per barrel at 1:06 p.m. ET on Wednesday, after touching its lowest level since September 4, with traders pricing an end to the Iran war after the White House tied Tuesday’s midterm losses to the conflict. WTI dropped $8.01, or 8.3%, to $88.08. Brent traded near $118 on Friday. Trump told Fox News on Tuesday night that “I think it’s the gasoline price” when explaining the Republican defeat. analysis.summary: Crude benchmarks plunge roughly 8-9% as U.S. political leadership links midterm election losses to the Iran war, fueling market bets on conflict de-escalation.
analysis.rationale: Executive branch statements blaming gas prices and conflict for electoral losses sparked rapid unwinding of geopolitical risk premiums, exerting strong and direct downward pressure on crude oil prices.

news.title: Africa’s LNG Exports Set to Soar 175% as Buyers Flee Hormuz
news.summary: Energy buyers burned by the Strait of Hormuz are turning to Africa, and the money is following. The African Energy Chamber projects that Africa’s upstream sector will attract ~$40 billion a year through 2030, lifting the continent’s hydrocarbon output to 12.5 MMboe/d. Mozambique, Nigeria, Angola, Libya and Ivory Coast will take the largest shares of that capital, while new projects in Uganda, Kenya and Namibia expand the production base. Major offshore discoveries and a wave of upstream deals are turning Africa into the world’s…

analysis.summary: Africa's upstream sector is projected to attract $40 billion annually through 2030, raising hydrocarbon output to 12.5 MMboe/d as buyers seek alternatives to Hormuz.
analysis.rationale: Long-term expansion of upstream hydrocarbon production capacity and alternative LNG supply from Africa tends to loosen global energy balances, applying downward price pressure.
